plan: Humanities passage (CLD-P-ACT-R-000064), an original essay on the restoration debate: Viollet-le-Duc at Notre-Dame and his definition of restoration, Ruskin's Seven Lamps (1849), Morris's Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings (1877, "Anti-Scrape"), the 2019 fire and the faithful rebuilding of the nineteenth-century spire (2024). Topic checked against every bank and the combined bank (no matches). Longer, argumentative passage with six items aimed at hard. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: A Lie from Beginning to End
passages.text:
By the 1840s, the cathedral of Notre-Dame in Paris was in poor condition. Revolutionaries had pulled down and beheaded the statues of its gallery of kings half a century earlier, its medieval spire had been taken down as unsafe in the 1780s, and decades of neglect had left its stone crumbling. Eugène Viollet-le-Duc, the architect best remembered for saving it, did far more than patch. He replaced lost sculptures with new ones of his own design, and he raised a tall new spire that the cathedral's medieval builders had never seen.

He was not embarrassed by these additions. "To restore a building," he later wrote, "is not to preserve it, to repair it, or to rebuild it; it is to reinstate it in a condition of completeness that could never have existed at any given time." The restorer, in his view, should understand a style so thoroughly that he could build what its original architects would have built had they possessed the means, or the time.

John Ruskin had already rejected this approach. In The Seven Lamps of Architecture (1849), he called restoration "the most total destruction which a building can suffer" and "a lie from beginning to end." For Ruskin, the value of an old building lay partly in the marks that centuries had left on it, such as the weathered carving and the worn step, and these could not be reproduced. A copy of a thirteenth-century capital carved in 1850 was a nineteenth-century capital, however exact. Better, he argued, to prop a building up with iron and timber, to tend it carefully, and, when it could no longer stand, to let it fall.

Ruskin's view found an institution in 1877, when William Morris founded the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings. Its members, nicknamed "Anti-Scrape" for their opposition to scraping the weathered surfaces of old buildings clean, urged owners to "put Protection in the place of Restoration." Their principles, to repair rather than replace and to let new work look new, shaped preservation practice for the next century.

In April 2019, fire destroyed Notre-Dame's roof and brought down Viollet-le-Duc's spire. The debate that followed would have been familiar to both men. Some proposed a bold modern spire; others insisted on rebuilding exactly what had fallen. France chose the second course, and in 2024 the cathedral reopened beneath a faithful copy of the nineteenth-century spire. There is an irony here that neither Ruskin nor Viollet-le-Duc could have foreseen: the restorer's invention, once a liberty taken with a medieval building, had itself become a piece of history worth preserving.

Perhaps that is the lesson. Ruskin was right that a copy cannot carry the years that made the original. But a building is not only a record of its first builders. It also records what each later generation believed the building should be, including, sometimes, a restorer's liberties.

candidates.stem: The passage as a whole is best described as:

choices.A: an argument that Viollet-le-Duc's additions to Notre-Dame should have been removed long ago.
choices.B: a biography of John Ruskin that focuses mainly on his writings about medieval architecture.
choices.C: an account of a restoration dispute that ends by treating later changes as history.
choices.D: a technical description of the methods used to rebuild the Notre-Dame spire after 2019.

candidates.evidence: It also records what each later generation believed the building should be
candidates.explanation: The passage traces the debate between Viollet-le-Duc's restoration and Ruskin's protection, then uses the 2019 fire to suggest that a restorer's additions can become part of a building's history.

A.rationale: The author never argues for removing his work and ends by treating it as history worth keeping.

B.rationale: Ruskin is one of several figures; the passage is about the restoration debate, not his life.

D.rationale: The rebuilding is mentioned briefly; no methods are described.

hints: Where does the passage end up?
candidates.remember: A main-idea answer must cover the whole passage, including its conclusion.

author_checklist.hardness: requires integrating the final two paragraphs

candidates.stem: According to the passage, Notre-Dame's medieval spire:

choices.A: was removed as unsafe before Viollet-le-Duc's work.
choices.B: was destroyed in the fire of April 2019.
choices.C: was rebuilt by Viollet-le-Duc to its first design.
choices.D: was pulled down by revolutionaries in the 1790s.

candidates.evidence: its medieval spire had been taken down as unsafe in the 1780s
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the medieval spire was taken down as unsafe in the 1780s, decades before Viollet-le-Duc's work in the 1840s.

B.rationale: The 2019 fire destroyed Viollet-le-Duc's spire, not the medieval one.

C.rationale: His spire was one the medieval builders had never seen.

D.rationale: The revolutionaries attacked the statues; the spire was removed as unsafe.

candidates.remember: Track which of two similar things a detail refers to.

candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 2, Viollet-le-Duc's phrase "a condition of completeness that could never have existed at any given time" most nearly suggests that:

choices.A: a restorer should return a building exactly to its first form.
choices.B: a building can never be fully repaired once it is damaged.
choices.C: medieval builders always left their buildings unfinished.
choices.D: a restored building may show a finished state it never had.

candidates.evidence: is to reinstate it in a condition of completeness that could never have existed at any given time
candidates.explanation: Viollet-le-Duc says restoration produces a complete state that could never have existed at any one time, so the restored building may look finished in a way it never was.

A.rationale: He says restoring is not merely preserving or rebuilding; it creates a state that never existed.

B.rationale: The phrase describes what restoration achieves, not a limit on repair.

C.rationale: The phrase does not claim that every medieval building was left unfinished.

hints: What did he add to Notre-Dame?

strategy.explanation: Connect the quotation to his additions.

candidates.remember: Interpret a quotation in light of the actions it explains.

author_checklist.hardness: abstract phrasing with a reverse trap

candidates.stem: Based on the passage, Ruskin would most likely regard a newly carved, exact copy of a weathered medieval statue as:

choices.A: an acceptable substitute, as long as the copy is exact.
choices.B: a new work that cannot carry the history of the original.
choices.C: more valuable than the original, because it is complete.
choices.D: a useful record of what the first builders intended.

candidates.evidence: was a nineteenth-century capital, however exact
candidates.explanation: Ruskin says a copy carved in 1850 is a nineteenth-century work however exact, because the marks of the centuries cannot be reproduced.

A.rationale: Ruskin says a copy is a new capital "however exact."

C.rationale: Ruskin valued the marks of age, not completeness.

D.rationale: This reflects Viollet-le-Duc's view, not Ruskin's.

hints: What did Ruskin say about an exact copy of a capital?

strategy.explanation: Apply his capital example to the statue.

candidates.remember: Apply a stated view to a parallel case.

candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 3, the word tend most nearly means:
candidates.explanation: Ruskin's advice is to look after the building carefully, so "tend" means "care for."

A.rationale: This is the meaning in "tend to," which does not fit "tend it carefully."

C.rationale: The building is not being moved toward anything.

D.rationale: "Serve" fits tending a shop or customers, not maintaining a building.

hints: Replace the word with each choice.

strategy.explanation: Substitute each choice into the sentence.

candidates.remember: Choose the meaning that fits the context, not the most familiar one.

candidates.stem: The author mentions the nickname "Anti-Scrape" (paragraph 4) mainly to:

choices.A: suggest that the society's members cared mostly about cleaning.
choices.B: imply that Morris disagreed with Ruskin about old surfaces.
choices.C: mock the society's members for being too cautious.
choices.D: show which restoration practice the society's members opposed.

candidates.evidence: for their opposition to scraping the weathered surfaces of old buildings clean
candidates.explanation: The passage explains that the nickname came from the members' opposition to scraping old surfaces clean.

A.rationale: The members opposed scraping surfaces clean.

B.rationale: The society put Ruskin's view into practice.

C.rationale: The author reports the nickname without mocking it.

hints: What does the passage say the nickname came from?

strategy.explanation: Read the explanation right after the nickname.

candidates.remember: The function of a detail is often explained in the same sentence.

candidates.stem: The passage indicates that the relationship between Ruskin's writing and Morris's society is that the society:

choices.A: turned Ruskin's view into an organized set of principles.
choices.B: rejected Ruskin's view that weathered surfaces should be kept.
choices.D: was founded before The Seven Lamps of Architecture.

candidates.evidence: Ruskin's view found an institution in 1877
candidates.explanation: The passage says Ruskin's view "found an institution" in Morris's society, whose principles carried that view into practice.

B.rationale: The society opposed scraping weathered surfaces, as Ruskin would.

C.rationale: The society urged protection in place of restoration.

D.rationale: The book appeared in 1849; the society was founded in 1877.

strategy.explanation: Paraphrase the first sentence of paragraph 4.

candidates.remember: Look for phrases that state a relationship directly.

candidates.stem: The irony described in paragraph 5 is that:

choices.A: the fire destroyed a spire that Ruskin had wished to save.
choices.B: France built a modern spire that both men would have rejected.
choices.C: a spire once seen as a liberty taken was rebuilt as history.
choices.D: the original medieval spire was rebuilt after centuries.

candidates.evidence: had itself become a piece of history worth preserving
candidates.explanation: Viollet-le-Duc's spire was once an invention imposed on a medieval building, yet after 2019 it was rebuilt exactly because it had become historic.

A.rationale: Ruskin opposed restorers' additions; the passage does not say he wished to save this spire.

B.rationale: France rebuilt a faithful copy, not a modern spire.

D.rationale: The rebuilt spire copies Viollet-le-Duc's nineteenth-century design.

hints: Whose spire was rebuilt, and why?

strategy.explanation: State the irony in your own words first.

candidates.remember: Irony is a reversal of what would be expected.

author_checklist.hardness: requires tracking which spire and why it was copied

candidates.stem: The final paragraph suggests that the author regards Ruskin's position as:

choices.A: mistaken, because a careful copy can carry the years of the original.
choices.B: fully persuasive, because restorers should never add new work.
choices.C: irrelevant, because Notre-Dame's spire was not medieval.
choices.D: right about copies but too narrow about what a building records.

candidates.evidence: Ruskin was right that a copy cannot carry the years that made the original
candidates.explanation: The author grants Ruskin's point about copies but adds that a building also records later generations' ideas, a point Ruskin's view leaves out.

A.rationale: The author says Ruskin was right that a copy cannot carry those years.

B.rationale: The author treats a restorer's liberties as part of a building's record.

C.rationale: The author engages with Ruskin's view rather than dismissing it.

hints: What does the author grant, and what does the author add?
candidates.remember: Watch for a concession followed by a qualification.

candidates.stem: As presented in the passage, Ruskin's rejection of restoration in The Seven Lamps of Architecture was published:

choices.B: in response to Viollet-le-Duc's quoted definition.
choices.C: after the founding of Morris's society.
choices.D: in the same year that Morris founded his society.

candidates.evidence: John Ruskin had already rejected this approach
candidates.explanation: Viollet-le-Duc "later wrote" his definition, and Ruskin "had already rejected" the approach in 1849, so Ruskin's book came first.

B.rationale: The passage says Ruskin had already rejected the approach and that Viollet-le-Duc wrote his definition later.

C.rationale: The book appeared in 1849, before the society's founding in 1877.

D.rationale: The book appeared in 1849; the society was founded in 1877.

hints: What do "later wrote" and "had already" tell you?

strategy.explanation: Use time words to order events.

candidates.remember: Order events from time signals, not from the order in which they are mentioned.
